guidance_note: This is an independent editorial summary based on official sources checked on 6 November 2026. Preparation guidance is not an additional eligibility rule. Applicants must confirm the current organiser terms, forms, deadlines, location rules and funding conditions before applying.

entries.title: ECoWYERT South Africa: Regional Trade Training for Youth, Entrepreneurs and Businesses
entries.organisation: United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) / Mastercard Foundation
entries.sectors: Youth enterprise, women-led enterprise, regional trade, AfCFTA, agribusiness, processing, services and cross-border commerce
entries.summary: Young people, entrepreneurs, traders and enterprises in South Africa can apply on a rolling basis for practical business, export-readiness and regional-trade training under the ECoWYERT programme.
entries.support: Business planning, financial management, marketing, digital business, formalisation, export-readiness and AfCFTA market-access training; no guaranteed cash grant
entries.deadline_label: Rolling applications; no fixed closing date stated on the current UNDP South Africa call
benefits: Stage-appropriate enterprise training covering business planning, financial management, marketing, customer development and digital business tools.
Regional trade and export-readiness support for established businesses seeking to enter or expand across African markets under AfCFTA.
Business formalisation and market-access guidance for micro, small, home-based, processing and growth-oriented enterprises.
eligibility: Applicants should be based in South Africa and select the programme category that best matches their current employment, business or trade stage.

The current call includes young people preparing for employment or entrepreneurship, micro and small businesses, home-based enterprises, processors, medium enterprises, aggregators and growth-oriented firms.
Applicants should provide complete and accurate information; submission does not guarantee selection and only shortlisted applicants are contacted.
conditions: The call describes training and enterprise support, not a guaranteed grant, investment or procurement contract.
Programme delivery and cohort timing may change while rolling applications remain open; verify the current intake before committing travel or staff time.
Use the official UNDP page to reach the current application form and avoid third-party intermediaries claiming guaranteed selection.
steps: Choose the category that best reflects your current business or employment stage.
Prepare a concise description of the enterprise, products or services, customers, current markets and the regional-trade barrier you want the programme to help address.
Submit through the application link published by UNDP South Africa and retain your submission confirmation.
entries.notice: This is a rolling training and enterprise-support opportunity. It should not be represented as a cash grant or guaranteed financing facility.
sources: UNDP South Africa official ECoWYERT application call

guide.context: ECoWYERT is a multi-country programme led by UNDP with the Mastercard Foundation and regional partners to strengthen the participation of women- and youth-led enterprises in regional trade under the African Continental Free Trade Area. The South Africa call is structured around practical business capability rather than a one-off prize. Participants are grouped by stage so a home-based enterprise is not expected to present the same readiness as an established exporter. That makes the programme potentially useful for businesses that need stronger management systems, clearer market positioning or a pathway into cross-border trade.
guide.fit: A strong fit is an applicant that can explain where the business is now and what specific capability gap is limiting growth. For an early-stage enterprise, that might be bookkeeping, customer development or formalisation. For a more established company, it might be export documentation, supply-chain reliability or understanding regional buyers. Applicants should avoid presenting the programme as a substitute for a functioning business model; the value is in strengthening the enterprise so it can participate more effectively in markets.
prepare: Summarise the business model, ownership, current customers, employment and the products or services being sold.
Identify the most important operational or regional-trade bottleneck and the evidence that it is constraining growth.
Prepare any registration, ownership, location or business-stage information requested by the current application form.
guide.strategy: Use the application to show progression rather than aspiration alone. If the enterprise already trades domestically, explain what has prevented regional expansion and which neighbouring or continental markets are realistic. If it is still informal, explain the path toward formalisation and reliable records. Women- and youth-led businesses should state ownership and decision-making clearly rather than relying on broad labels. The strongest application is likely to connect the training to a practical next step such as improved records, a new buyer pipeline, export readiness or better use of digital sales channels.
guide.commitment: Because applications are rolling, do not assume immediate admission. Cohorts can fill and implementation arrangements can change. Keep copies of submitted information and verify any later request for documents through official programme channels. Participation does not guarantee finance, contracts or market entry. Treat the programme as capability development and continue evaluating the commercial economics of regional expansion independently.

entries.title: ECoWYERT Zimbabwe: Regional Trade Training for Youth, Entrepreneurs and Businesses
entries.organisation: United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) / Mastercard Foundation
entries.sectors: Youth enterprise, women-led enterprise, regional trade, AfCFTA, agribusiness, processing and cross-border commerce
entries.summary: Zimbabwean young people, entrepreneurs, traders and enterprises can apply on a rolling basis for practical business and regional-trade training through the ECoWYERT programme.
entries.support: Business-management, financial literacy, digital business, formalisation, market-access and export-readiness training; no guaranteed cash grant
entries.deadline_label: Rolling applications; no fixed closing date stated on the current UNDP Zimbabwe call
benefits: Practical training in business planning, financial literacy, management and record keeping.
Marketing, customer-development and digital selling skills for enterprises at different stages.
Regional-market and AfCFTA export-readiness guidance for growth-oriented firms and aggregators.
eligibility: Applicants should be in Zimbabwe and select the category that best describes their current employment, business or trade stage.
The published categories include micro and small businesses, home-based enterprises, small-scale processors, medium enterprises, formal firms, aggregators and growth-oriented businesses.
Applications must be complete and accurate; submission does not guarantee selection.
conditions: The published opportunity is training and enterprise development rather than an automatic grant or investment.
Only shortlisted applicants are contacted, and rolling intake does not mean immediate admission.
Applicants should use the current official UNDP page and linked form rather than paying intermediaries.
steps: Select the correct applicant category and describe the present stage of the enterprise.
Prepare basic information on customers, products, markets, records and the regional-trade capability you want to strengthen.
Submit through the official form linked from UNDP Zimbabwe and retain evidence of submission.
entries.notice: Applications are rolling. The programme does not guarantee selection, financing or export contracts.
sources: UNDP Zimbabwe official ECoWYERT application page

guide.context: The Zimbabwe ECoWYERT call is part of the same six-country regional initiative operating in Botswana, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Malawi, South Africa, Zambia and Zimbabwe. Its practical focus is to help young people and women-led or youth-led enterprises participate more effectively in cross-border commerce. The training spans foundational business capability through export readiness, so applicants should choose the track that reflects their actual stage instead of overstating maturity.
guide.fit: A useful fit is an entrepreneur or enterprise that can identify a concrete gap between its current capability and the requirements of a larger or regional market. A processor may need better records and quality systems; a trader may need stronger market intelligence; an established enterprise may need supply-chain and export planning. Applicants who are still at the idea stage should check whether the current category explicitly supports that level before presenting themselves as an operating business.
prepare: Document the current products or services, customer base, ownership and team size.
Identify one or two measurable improvements you want from the programme, such as stronger financial records or a regional buyer pipeline.
Keep registration and identity information consistent across the application and any later due-diligence request.
guide.strategy: Regional trade is not only about finding a buyer. The enterprise may need reliable production, quality control, logistics, pricing, payment systems and working capital. A strong application should demonstrate awareness of those requirements and show which ones the programme can realistically help address. Avoid claiming that AfCFTA automatically removes every border, standard or documentation requirement. The value of the programme is in preparing the enterprise to navigate those systems more effectively.
guide.commitment: Rolling applications can remain open while cohorts are processed in stages. Applicants should monitor the official page and contact details for updates rather than assuming silence means rejection. No programme description should be interpreted as a promise of financing or guaranteed market access. Any later finance or partnership offer should be assessed on its own terms.

entries.title: IFAD Crisis Response Grants for Farmers’ Organizations: Up to US$250,000
entries.sectors: Smallholder agriculture, farmer organisations, inputs, small-scale infrastructure, finance, markets and rural resilience
entries.summary: Eligible national and large sub-national farmers’ organizations in selected crisis-affected countries can apply for one of two IFAD grants of up to US$250,000 for rapid resilience interventions.
entries.support: Up to US$250,000 per selected project; IFAD expects to support two projects from a total US$500,000 envelope
entries.deadline_label: 20 November 2026; the official page states the date but does not state a cutoff time
entries.countries: Malawi, Ethiopia, South Sudan, Mozambique, Sudan, Somalia, Mali, Burkina Faso, Nigeria and Chad; the wider call also includes selected countries outside Africa
benefits: Grant financing of up to US$250,000 for a maximum 12-month implementation period.
Support for one primary Crisis Response Initiative pillar: inputs and production support, small-scale infrastructure, access to finance, or access to markets and market information.
An opportunity for established farmers’ organizations to deliver rapid, locally rooted responses to compounded rural crises.
eligibility: Legally registered, non-profit, national or large sub-national farmers’ organization with a direct membership base composed primarily of smallholder producers.
Previous experience managing grant resources and prior satisfactory participation in specified IFAD farmers’ organization grant programmes.
Adequate governance, financial management, procurement and internal controls, recent audited financial statements, relevant operational experience and a presence in the target area.
conditions: Applicants may submit under only one primary CRI pillar and must deliver measurable results within a maximum 12-month implementation period.
Project-management costs may not exceed 20% of the grant amount.
This is not an open grant for any NGO or agribusiness; the farmers’ organization and prior-IFAD-experience criteria are material eligibility gates.
steps: Confirm that the organisation and target country satisfy the farmers’ organization, prior IFAD programme and geographic requirements.
Prepare the required concept note, results framework, activity-based budget, financial-management questionnaire and self-certification.
Submit using the official IFAD instructions by 20 November 2026 and retain all submitted documents and correspondence.
entries.notice: The call has strict institutional eligibility requirements. An organisation that has not previously participated satisfactorily in the specified IFAD farmers’ organisation programmes should not assume it is eligible.
sources: IFAD official Crisis Response farmers’ organisations call

guide.context: This IFAD call is unusually specific: it is designed for established farmers’ organizations with prior experience under named IFAD-supported farmers’ organization programmes, not for general NGOs, individual farmers or ordinary private companies. The funding responds to overlapping shocks affecting smallholders and is intended for rapid implementation. The African priority countries are Malawi, Ethiopia, South Sudan, Mozambique, Sudan, Somalia, Mali, Burkina Faso, Nigeria and Chad.
guide.fit: A strong fit is a farmers’ organization that already has a functioning membership base, audited systems, a track record with donor funds and an operational presence in one of the target countries. The proposed intervention should concentrate on one primary pillar and solve a clearly evidenced crisis-related constraint within one year. A proposal that tries to cover every possible problem will be weaker than one with a focused delivery mechanism and credible beneficiary reach.
prepare: Verify the organisation’s previous participation and satisfactory performance in FO4ACP, FO4Asia, FO4Latin America or FO4IMPACT as required by the call.
Assemble current audited statements, governance and procurement evidence before drafting the technical concept.
Choose one primary CRI pillar and build the results framework and budget around measurable outputs achievable within 12 months.
guide.strategy: The call rewards delivery capacity as much as a good idea. Explain how the organisation reaches members, how inputs or finance will move, how procurement will be controlled, and how results can be verified quickly. For market-access proposals, show the actual market failure and the mechanism that will improve resilience. For infrastructure, keep the intervention community-scale as required. The budget should be proportionate to the delivery model rather than simply targeting the maximum award.
guide.commitment: Because the call requires rapid implementation, applicants should assess whether staff, procurement systems and local partnerships can mobilise quickly after award. Do not submit if the organisation cannot satisfy the prior IFAD participation condition. The date is official, but the page does not state a cutoff time, so applicants should submit well before 20 November rather than assuming midnight.

entries.title: UNIDO Global Call for Sustainable Industrial AI-Powered Solutions
entries.organisation: UNIDO, UNCTAD, ITU and partner UN organisations
entries.sectors: Artificial intelligence, manufacturing, industrial robotics, digital infrastructure, green industry, data, finance, skills and market access
entries.summary: Startups, MSMEs, technology companies, research organisations and other solution providers from developing and middle-income economies can submit industrial AI solutions for global showcasing and matchmaking.
entries.support: Selected solutions receive exhibition visibility, solution talks, workshops, matchmaking and inclusion in the AIM Global solutions repository; no cash award is stated
entries.deadline_label: 9 November 2026; the official UNIDO announcement states the date but not a cutoff time
entries.countries: Open to solution providers addressing developing and middle-income economies, including African countries
benefits: Opportunity for selected solutions to be showcased at the AIM Global Action Forum in Vienna on 25–26 November 2026.
Exhibition space, solution talks, workshop participation and dedicated matchmaking for selected providers.
Longer-term visibility through the AIM Global solutions repository and Centres of Excellence network.
eligibility: Solution providers of different sizes and types, including startups, MSMEs, established technology companies, research organisations and international or regional organisations.
AI-powered solutions should address real industrial needs in developing and middle-income economies.
The call accepts different maturity levels, from emerging innovations to deployable and flagship solutions.
conditions: The official announcement does not state a cash grant for selected solutions.
Applicants should classify solution maturity accurately and provide evidence appropriate to the selected category.
Selection for showcasing or matchmaking is not a procurement or investment guarantee.
steps: Select the most appropriate industrial AI thematic track and maturity category.
Prepare concise evidence of the industrial problem, technical solution, users, deployment maturity, measured results and scalability.
Submit through the official UNIDO call before 9 November 2026.
entries.notice: This is a visibility, demonstration and matchmaking call rather than a stated cash-grant programme.
sources: UNIDO official global industrial AI call

guide.context: The call is designed to identify industrial AI solutions that can move beyond generic demonstrations into real industrial use. UNIDO and its partners explicitly recognise different maturity levels, which allows an emerging innovation to be assessed differently from an already deployed system. African providers can use the opportunity to demonstrate solutions relevant to manufacturing, industrial infrastructure, green production, data systems, finance or skills in developing-market conditions.
guide.fit: A strong fit is a solution with a specific industrial user and problem, not a general AI platform searching for an application. Applicants should be able to explain why AI is necessary, what data or operating environment the solution depends on, and what evidence exists that it works. Solutions designed for limited connectivity, smaller firms or resource-constrained settings may be especially relevant to many African industrial contexts.
prepare: Define the exact industrial workflow or bottleneck addressed and identify the intended user.
Prepare evidence of technical maturity, deployments or pilots, measured performance and responsible-AI controls.
Choose the correct maturity category rather than overstating readiness for scale.
guide.strategy: The application should connect technology to industrial value: lower downtime, better quality, reduced energy use, safer operations, stronger supply chains or improved market access. Avoid vague claims that AI will transform an industry. Show what changes in the process, who uses the system and how outcomes are measured. If the solution is still emerging, be explicit about the validation still required. If it is deployable, provide credible implementation evidence.
guide.commitment: The submission window is short. Applicants should verify any travel, exhibition or participation arrangements if selected and should not assume travel costs or financing are covered unless the organiser confirms them. Matchmaking can create opportunities but is not a guarantee of procurement, investment or partnership.

entries.title: Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program at Cambridge 2027/28
entries.sectors: Postgraduate education, climate resilience, sustainability, leadership and development
entries.summary: African citizens resident in Africa can apply for fully funded eligible one-year Master’s programmes at the University of Cambridge for 2027/28, with the scholarship application integrated into the course application.
entries.support: Full tuition plus maintenance, visa, travel and related scholarship support under the programme terms
entries.deadline_label: Course-specific funding deadline, usually early December 2026 or early January 2027; applicants must use the funding deadline for their chosen course
benefits: Full tuition support for eligible full-time one-year Master’s programmes.
Maintenance support plus visa and travel costs under the scholarship terms.
Leadership development and a community focused on sustainability and climate resilience in Africa.
eligibility: Citizen of an African country and resident in an African country, subject to the programme’s temporary-absence exceptions.
Bachelor’s degree and the academic entry requirements for the chosen Cambridge course.
Apply to an eligible full-time Master’s; MBA, MCL, MFin and MAcc are excluded from the programme.
conditions: The scholarship is integrated into the Cambridge course application and applicants must opt in for funding where eligible.
The deadline is course-specific and is the course’s funding deadline, not the later standard admissions deadline.
Applicants must demonstrate commitment to giving back to their community, home country or Africa and alignment with sustainability and climate resilience.
steps: Identify an eligible full-time one-year Master’s course and confirm its academic and funding deadline.
Prepare the Cambridge course application and scholarship statement covering career history, leadership, goals and contribution to sustainable futures in Africa.
Submit by the chosen course’s funding deadline and complete any fee-waiver process early where relevant.
entries.notice: There is no single programme-wide closing date. The relevant deadline is the funding deadline of the selected Cambridge course, commonly in early December or early January.
sources: Cambridge Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program — applications open
Cambridge Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program — how to apply

guide.context: The Cambridge Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program is a fully funded postgraduate route for African students, with a particular emphasis on leadership, climate resilience and sustainability. The scholarship is not a separate first-stage application: candidates apply for an eligible Cambridge Master’s course and indicate the funding option within that application. This makes course selection and academic fit central to the process.
guide.fit: A strong applicant should meet the academic standard of the chosen course and be able to connect past experience, leadership and future plans to a credible contribution in Africa. Climate resilience and sustainability are broad programme themes, so applicants from many disciplines can fit if they can explain how their study and leadership trajectory connect to sustainable futures. The excluded professional degrees should not be selected in expectation of scholarship coverage.
prepare: Shortlist eligible courses by academic fit first, then confirm each course’s funding deadline.
Prepare transcripts, references, CV and the scholarship statement well before the funding deadline.
If an application fee is a barrier, use the programme’s fee-waiver route early and observe its stated timing.
guide.strategy: The scholarship statement should complement rather than repeat the academic application. Explain what problem you want to work on, how your previous experience demonstrates leadership or service, and why the Cambridge course is the right next step. Avoid generic claims about changing Africa. A specific, evidence-backed trajectory is more persuasive: what you have already done, what capability you need, and what you plan to do with it.
guide.commitment: Because deadlines differ by course, applicants must manage the application as a course-specific project. Do not wait for a single scholarship deadline. Review the funding deadline shown in the Cambridge course directory, submit early enough for references and document checks, and keep evidence of submission. Funding is highly competitive and a course offer does not automatically guarantee a scholarship.

entries.title: UNDP–IEEE GenAI for Good Challenge: Cities Edition
entries.organisation: United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) / IEEE Humanitarian Technologies
entries.sectors: Generative AI, public transport, energy efficiency, urban planning, green infrastructure and open-source civic technology
entries.summary: Teams of technologists and innovators worldwide can apply to co-develop open-source GenAI solutions for municipal challenges in Pristina, Rivne and Skopje, with prototype and pilot funding.
entries.support: Nine prototype teams receive US$10,000; up to three pilot teams can receive up to US$30,000 additional funding plus technical mentorship
entries.deadline_label: 13 December 2026; the official UNDP announcement states the date but not a cutoff time
entries.countries: Open worldwide, including teams based in African countries; solutions address city challenges in Kosovo, Ukraine and North Macedonia
benefits: US$10,000 for each of nine teams selected to build prototypes.
Up to US$30,000 additional funding for teams selected to pilot solutions with a participating city.
Direct collaboration with city stakeholders plus technical mentorship from IEEE and development/public-sector support from UNDP.
eligibility: Teams of technologists and innovators worldwide are invited to apply.
Applicants must complete the required technical assessment and narrative proposal.
Solutions should address one of the published city challenges and be suitable for responsible, open-source development and municipal testing.
conditions: The challenge is global but the implementation problems are tied to the three specified cities.
Up to three solutions proceed to pilots; prototype selection does not guarantee additional pilot funding.
Open-source code and documentation are part of the programme’s intended reuse model.
steps: Choose the city challenge that best matches the team’s technical and domain capability.
Complete the technical assessment and prepare a narrative explaining the proposed GenAI approach, responsible-use safeguards and implementation plan.
Submit through the application route linked from the official UNDP announcement before 13 December 2026.
entries.notice: African teams can apply, but the challenge problems and pilots are based in the three named European and Central Asian cities.
sources: UNDP official GenAI for Good Cities Edition announcement

guide.context: This challenge is relevant to African technologists because participation is worldwide and the problems—public transport planning, energy-efficiency investment and green-infrastructure management—also resemble challenges facing many African cities. The immediate pilots, however, are in Pristina, Rivne and Skopje. Applicants should therefore solve the published city problem first rather than turning the application into a proposal for a different geography.
guide.fit: A strong team combines AI engineering with enough domain understanding to work with municipal data and public-sector users. The proposal should demonstrate responsible GenAI design, not simply a chatbot interface. Explain data limitations, verification, human oversight, multilingual needs, privacy and how the municipal user will judge whether the tool improves a real decision.
prepare: Study the selected city challenge and identify the specific municipal workflow the solution must improve.
Prepare a technical architecture, data assumptions, responsible-AI safeguards and a realistic prototype plan.
Clarify team roles and prior evidence of building deployable software, civic technology or domain-relevant systems.
guide.strategy: The strongest proposal should be narrow enough to prototype and useful enough for a city to test. Do not promise a universal urban AI platform. Focus on the task, users, data and measurable improvement. Because the programme requires open-source outputs, the architecture should separate reusable components from any city-sensitive data. Show how the solution can be maintained after the challenge rather than depending entirely on the competition team.
guide.commitment: Teams should budget time for collaborative work with city stakeholders and possible pilot iterations. The US$10,000 prototype award is not the same as the later pilot award, and not all prototype teams advance. Applicants should verify the detailed terms on the linked challenge platform before accepting intellectual-property, open-source, travel or reporting obligations.

entries.title: IsDB Competitive Technology Sourcing: Soil Stabilisation and Rural Solar
entries.sectors: Road engineering, soil stabilisation, rural solar, infrastructure, clean energy and technology deployment
entries.summary: Commercialisation-ready technology providers can submit proven soil-stabilisation or rural solar solutions for possible due diligence and future deployment across IsDB member countries.
entries.support: Shortlisting, due diligence and potential introduction for deployment under IsDB’s Technology Deployment Cooperation Program; no guaranteed financing or procurement
entries.deadline_label: 15 November 2026; the official IsDB page states the closing date but not a cutoff time
entries.countries: Technology providers can apply internationally; solutions are intended for IsDB member countries, including member countries across Africa
benefits: Opportunity for qualifying technology providers to enter IsDB technical assessment and due diligence.
Potential introduction of shortlisted technologies for deployment in IsDB member-country projects.
Visibility for mature solutions in rural roads or solar energy that have strong commercial traction.
eligibility: Technology companies, startups, research centres, universities and institutions with commercialisation-ready intellectual property can participate.
Solutions should be practical, scalable, proven in operation and adaptable to member-country needs.
The current page states an expected deployment track record of at least three clients with total sales of at least US$20 million.
conditions: The exercise is exploratory and non-binding; participation does not guarantee selection, financing or procurement.
Applicants should review the separate technical brief for the soil-stabilisation or solar track before submitting.
The strong commercial track-record requirement makes this unsuitable for most idea-stage or early prototype ventures.
steps: Choose the soil-stabilisation or rural-solar technology track and review the technical brief.
Prepare evidence of deployments, clients, total commercial sales, technical performance, costs, scalability and environmental/social value.
Submit through the official IsDB page before 15 November 2026.
entries.notice: This is a market-sounding and technology-sourcing exercise, not a grant award or guaranteed procurement process.
sources: IsDB official Competitive Technology Sourcing page

guide.context: IsDB is using this sourcing exercise to identify technologies that are mature enough for possible deployment across member-country development projects. The two current tracks are soil stabilisation for roads and innovative solar energy for rural communities. The opportunity is therefore closer to technology sourcing and market access than to a startup competition.
guide.fit: A strong fit is a provider with substantial real-world deployment evidence, commercial traction and the capacity to support implementation in new geographies. The official page sets a demanding reference point: at least three clients and total sales of at least US$20 million. Early-stage startups without that level of proof should not spend time treating this as a seed-funding call.
prepare: Map existing deployments directly against the technical requirements in the selected IsDB brief.
Prepare verifiable client references, sales evidence, technical performance data and lifecycle-cost information.
Explain how the solution can be adapted to infrastructure, climate, maintenance and local-capacity conditions in IsDB member countries.
guide.strategy: The proposal should make commercial maturity visible. IsDB is not simply looking for an inventive technology; it is looking for something that can withstand due diligence and potentially be deployed. Use quantified evidence on cost, reliability, maintenance, environmental performance and delivery capacity. For solar, explain affordability and the business or service model. For roads, explain engineering performance and quality control.
guide.commitment: Shortlisting leads to further assessment, not a contract. Providers should be prepared for technical and commercial due diligence and should protect confidential information appropriately while still supplying enough evidence for assessment. Confirm all later procurement or partnership terms independently before committing resources.
